title: 1492 and after
hookLine: Granada falls, and the Muslims of Spain are later forced to convert or leave

cards: South of Granada there's a mountain pass whose name is really a story: the sigh of the Moor.

People tell that the sultan who handed Granada over, Abu Abdallah, whom the Spanish called Boabdil, rode out with his household, stopped at that pass, turned for one last look at the city and the red palace, and wept.
Whether he wept there, nobody can say for certain. What came after his surrender is better documented, and it is harder to hear.

teach.b: Granada did not fall in a final battle.

It was surrendered by treaty to Ferdinand and Isabella, the Catholic monarchs of Spain, and the treaty made promises: Muslims could keep their mosques, their faith, their law, their property. Those promises did not last.

Before long the authorities were pressing Muslims to be baptized, and in time, across Spain, the choice became baptism or exile. Families who stayed, because home was home, were baptized, and came to be called Moriscos.
Some became sincere Christians. Others kept Islam in secret, praying behind closed doors, teaching children quietly. And they wrote.
Some Moriscos wrote Spanish in Arabic letters, copying prayers, stories of the prophets and rules of worship in a script their neighbors couldn't read.
A language hiding inside another, so that faith could survive in a kitchen. The suspicion never lifted. There were rebellions, crushed.

teach.h: EXPELLED, AS THE JEWS HAD BEEN.
teach.b: In the end the Moriscos as a whole, even those who were truly Christian, were expelled from Spain, crossing to North Africa and beyond. Their neighbors had been through it already.
In the same year Granada surrendered, the Jews of Spain were ordered to convert or leave, and Jewish families left. Two communities, the same choice.
This closes the walk through al-Andalus, and this ending belongs in the story too, beside the arches and the books.

how: The loss of al-Andalus and the expulsion of the Moriscos are remembered in Muslim histories, poetry and sermons; some families in North Africa trace their roots to the Moriscos.

games.q: you're a Muslim family in Spain after the surrender. the promises have broken, and the choice is baptism or exile. what did families like yours do?
o: all of them left at once.
some stayed and were baptized, and some of those kept Islam in secret.
games.why: families stayed, because home was home. baptized, they were called Moriscos; some became Christians, others kept Islam behind closed doors, until the expulsion came anyway.

practice: Think of a family made to leave a home they loved, the Moriscos at a harbor, or people forced from their homes today, and picture one ordinary thing they had to leave behind: a door key, a kitchen, a tree in a yard.
Stay with that one thing. If you pray, remember them in whatever words are already yours; if you don't, keep them company in your attention.

wordCard.voice: Moriscos. The Muslims who stayed in Spain after Granada surrendered in fourteen ninety-two, forced to convert and, in the end, expelled. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: al-Andalus, the name Muslims gave the lands they ruled in Spain and Portugal.

carryVoice: Your line: remember the moriscos. Faith survived in kitchens and in hidden letters. See you tomorrow.
